**Proof.** Yes, the reversed form holds. We derive it from the standard Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder by a change of variables.

Recall the standard form: if $g$ is $\mathcal{C}^n([a,b])$ and $n+1$ times differentiable on $(a,b)$, there exists $\xi\in(a,b)$ such that
$$g(b)=g(a)+g'(a)(b-a)+\frac{g''(a)}{2!}(b-a)^2+\cdots+\frac{g^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(b-a)^n+\frac{g^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(b-a)^{n+1}.$$

Apply this to the function $g(x):=f(a+b-x)$ on $[a,b]$. Since $f$ is $\mathcal{C}^n([a,b])$ and $n+1$ times differentiable, so is $g$. By the chain rule,
$$g^{(k)}(x)=(-1)^k f^{(k)}(a+b-x),\qquad k=0,1,\dots,n+1.$$
In particular,
$$g(a)=f(b),\quad g(b)=f(a),\quad g^{(k)}(a)=(-1)^k f^{(k)}(b).$$

Substituting into the standard Taylor formula for $g$ gives, for some $\xi\in(a,b)$:
$$f(a)=f(b)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k f^{(k)}(b)}{k!}(b-a)^k+\frac{(-1)^{n+1}f^{(n+1)}(a+b-\xi)}{(n+1)!}(b-a)^{n+1}.$$

Since $b-a=-(a-b)$, we have $(-1)^k(b-a)^k=(a-b)^k$. Setting $c:=a+b-\xi$, and noting that $\xi\in(a,b)$ implies $c\in(a,b)$, every term becomes
$$f(a)=f(b)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(b)}{k!}(a-b)^k+\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(a-b)^{n+1},$$
i.e.
$$f(a)=f(b)+f'(b)(a-b)+\cdots+\frac{f^{(n)}(b)}{n!}(a-b)^n+\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(a-b)^{n+1}$$
for some $c\in(a,b)$.

Thus Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder remains valid with the roles of $a$ and $b$ reversed; the only change is that the intermediate point $c$ is generally a different point (it is the reflection $a+b-\xi$ of the point $\xi$ obtained from the standard form). $\blacksquare$
